title: Why Is Coca-Cola Red? (It's Not Santa)

shots.vo: Quick question. Why is Coca-Cola red? If you just said Santa Claus, you are not alone.

shots.vo: The red came first. Decades first. And the real reason has nothing to do with Christmas. It has to do with tax collectors.

shots.vo: Think about how strange this is. A brown drink. In a red can.

shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Nothing about cola is red. Not the taste, not the color, not a single ingredient. And yet that one red is so powerful the company calls it its second secret formula.
shots.prompt: a perfectly round glossy red disc glowing on a dark brick wall at night, neon reflection on wet pavement, no text

shots.vo: So where did it come from?

shots.vo: Atlanta, eighteen eighty-six. A pharmacist named John Pemberton mixes a syrup and sells it at a soda fountain, five cents a glass.
shots.prompt: an 1880s American pharmacy soda fountain with marble counter, brass taps, glass jars, a pharmacist in a waistcoat mixing syrup, warm gaslight, oil painting style
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: His bookkeeper, Frank Robinson, names it. He writes the name in flowing script, and he paints the first signs in red letters on white. He simply liked how it popped.
shots.prompt: a 19th century bookkeeper with ink pen writing elegant script on paper at a wooden desk, red ink bottle, candlelight, close-up of hands, no readable words
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: But a color you like isn't a color you're stuck with. What locked it in?
shots.prompt: a dim 1890s brick warehouse full of stacked wooden barrels, beams of dusty light through high windows
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Here's the problem. In the eighteen nineties, the syrup travelled across America in wooden barrels. And so did whiskey.
shots.prompt: an 1890s steam freight train crossing open prairie at sunset, smoke trailing, wide cinematic view
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Alcohol was taxed. Soda was not. To a tax agent at a depot, one barrel looked exactly like the other.
shots.prompt: a busy 1890s railway depot platform stacked with identical brown wooden barrels, workers with hand carts, an official inspecting, hazy morning light
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: So, as the company tells it, they painted their barrels red. One look, and the agent knew: no whiskey here, no tax.
A red barrel rolling off every train, into every town, onto every soda fountain floor in the country.
shots.prompt: a single bright red wooden barrel being rolled off a freight car onto a wooden platform, dramatic low angle, warm light
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Red stopped being decoration. It became the signal. See red, and you knew the cold drink was here.
shots.prompt: an 1890s small-town main street with a general store, a bright red painted sign board above the door with no readable text, horse carriage, golden hour
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Now, Santa. In nineteen thirty-one, Coca-Cola hired an artist named Haddon Sundblom to paint Santa for its Christmas ads.
shots.prompt: an artist in a 1930s studio painting a jolly bearded man in a red suit on a large canvas, easel, oil paints, warm window light, seen from behind the artist
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Those paintings were everywhere, for decades. Plump, rosy, red suit. That's why so many people think Coke invented him.
shots.prompt: a 1930s American living room at Christmas with a fireplace, stockings, a magazine open on a table showing a painted Santa, cozy warm light, no readable text
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: But look at the dates. Red letters, eighteen eighty-six. Red barrels, the eighteen nineties. And in nineteen fifteen, sixteen years before Coke's Santa, a mineral water brand called White Rock was already selling with a red-suited Santa.
Artists had been dressing Santa in red for years. Even Coca-Cola's own archivists say it: Santa wore red before their ads.
shots.prompt: a stack of antique early 1900s Christmas postcards and magazine covers on a wooden table, Santa in red robes in illustrations, soft candlelight, no readable text
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: So Coke didn't make Santa red. If anything, a red Santa fit perfectly with a brand that was already red.
shots.prompt: a plain red soda can beside a small vintage Santa figurine on a snowy windowsill, night, warm glow from inside, no logo
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: Today that red is one of the most recognised colors on Earth. And here's the strange part: there's no official paint code for it. No standard swatch. When you see it, you just know.
shots.prompt: a giant red billboard panel glowing over a crowded neon city street at night, rain reflections, no text
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: All because, a hundred and thirty years ago, somebody had to tell soda from whiskey.
shots.prompt: a lone red wooden barrel in an empty old warehouse, a single beam of light falling on it, dust floating
shots.negative: logo, text, letters, words, brand, label, watermark

shots.vo: A tax rule, a bookkeeper's favorite color, and a coat of paint. That's the hidden why.
